claim: Most neurogenesis in the mammalian brain is completed embryonically.
source: Most neurogenesis in the mammalian brain is completed embryonically, but in certain areas the production of neurons continues throughout postnatal life.
evidence: This is a general statement about mammalian neurogenesis presented in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: In certain areas of the mammalian brain, the production of neurons continues throughout postnatal life.
source: Most neurogenesis in the mammalian brain is completed embryonically, but in certain areas the production of neurons continues throughout postnatal life.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about adult neurogenesis in specific brain regions.

claim: The functional properties of mature postnatally generated neurons often match those of their embryonically produced counterparts.
source: The functional properties of mature postnatally generated neurons often match those of their embryonically produced counterparts.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the abstract, setting up the contrast with the current findings.

claim: In the olfactory bulb, embryonic and postnatal neurogenesis produce functionally distinct subpopulations of dopaminergic neurons.
source: However, we show here that in the olfactory bulb (OB), embryonic and postnatal neurogenesis produce functionally distinct subpopulations of dopaminergic (DA) neurons.
evidence: This is the main claim of the study, supported by multiple experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Two subclasses of OB DA neurons can be defined by the presence or absence of the axon initial segment (AIS).
source: We define two subclasses of OB DA neuron by the presence or absence of a key subcellular specialisation: the axon initial segment (AIS).
evidence: This classification is based on immunohistochemical data showing AnkG labeling in a subset of DA neurons.

claim: Large AIS-positive axon-bearing DA neurons are exclusively produced during early embryonic stages.
source: Large AIS-positive axon-bearing DA neurons are exclusively produced during early embryonic stages, leaving small anaxonic AIS-negative cells as the only DA subtype generated via adult neurogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by BrdU birthdating experiments showing AIS-positive cells only when BrdU was injected at early embryonic timepoints.

claim: Small anaxonic AIS-negative cells are the only DA subtype generated via adult neurogenesis.
source: Large AIS-positive axon-bearing DA neurons are exclusively produced during early embryonic stages, leaving small anaxonic AIS-negative cells as the only DA subtype generated via adult neurogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by BrdU birthdating and electroporation experiments showing no AIS-positive cells generated postnatally or in adults.

claim: Large DA cells are more excitable than small DA cells.
source: These populations are functionally distinct: large DA cells are more excitable, yet display weaker and – for certain long-latency or inhibitory events – more broadly tuned responses to odorant stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings showing lower current threshold and higher maximum spike numbers in biphasic (large) cells.

claim: Large DA cells display weaker responses to odorant stimuli than small DA cells.
source: These populations are functionally distinct: large DA cells are more excitable, yet display weaker and – for certain long-latency or inhibitory events – more broadly tuned responses to odorant stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo GCaMP imaging data showing significantly lower response amplitudes in big cells across all response types.

claim: Large DA cells display more broadly tuned responses to odorant stimuli for certain long-latency or inhibitory events.
source: These populations are functionally distinct: large DA cells are more excitable, yet display weaker and – for certain long-latency or inhibitory events – more broadly tuned responses to odorant stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo GCaMP imaging showing higher tuning index values for late excitatory and inhibitory responses in big cells.

claim: Embryonic and postnatal neurogenesis can generate distinct neuronal subclasses.
source: Embryonic and postnatal neurogenesis can therefore generate distinct neuronal subclasses, placing important constraints on the functional roles of adult-born neurons in sensory processing.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined morphological, developmental, and functional data presented in the study.

claim: Neurogenic zones in the adult rodent brain give rise to hippocampal dentate granule cells and interneurons in the olfactory bulb.
source: Such neurogenic zones are small, spatially defined and give rise to two broad neuronal populations: hippocampal dentate granule cells, and interneurons in the olfactory bulb (OB) (Lledo et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lledo et al., 2006.

claim: Adult-generated neurons bring unique properties to existing networks by virtue of their transient immature status.
source: These newly generated cells are believed to bring unique properties to existing networks, largely by virtue of the specialised functional and plastic features associated with their transient immature status (e.g. Carleton et al., 2003; Ge et al., 2007; Gu et al., 2012; Livneh et al., 2014; Marín-Burgin and Schinder, 2012; Nissant et al., 2009; Schmidt-Hieber et al., 2004, but see Sailor et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Once fully mature, the functional properties of adult-generated neurons in both the hippocampus and olfactory bulb often closely match those of their developmentally generated neighbours.
source: Once fully mature, though, the functional properties of adult-generated neurons in both the hippocampus and olfactory bulb often closely match those of their developmentally generated neighbours (e.g. Carleton et al., 2003; Grubb et al., 2008; Laplagne et al., 2006; Marín-Burgin and Schinder, 2012; Nissant et al., 2009, but see Valley et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Glomerular layer interneurons modulate the earliest stages of sensory information processing in the olfactory bulb.
source: Among the wider population of adult-generated OB cells is a heterogeneous group of inhibitory neurons situated in the structure's glomerular layer, whose main role is to modulate the earliest stages of sensory information processing (Alonso et al., 2012; Fukunaga et al., 2014; Grubb et al., 2008; Livneh et al., 2014; Livneh and Mizrahi, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Different subclasses of glomerular layer interneuron can be identified by their specific expression of calcium-binding proteins.
source: Different subclasses of glomerular layer interneuron can be identified by their specific expression of calcium-binding proteins (Kosaka and Kosaka, 2011), while another major subclass is identified by its ability to co-release both GABA and dopamine (Borisovska et al., 2013; Vaaga et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kosaka and Kosaka, 2011.

claim: A major subclass of glomerular layer interneurons is identified by its ability to co-release both GABA and dopamine.
source: Different subclasses of glomerular layer interneuron can be identified by their specific expression of calcium-binding proteins (Kosaka and Kosaka, 2011), while another major subclass is identified by its ability to co-release both GABA and dopamine (Borisovska et al., 2013; Vaaga et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Borisovska et al., 2013 and Vaaga et al., 2017.

claim: Dopaminergic interneurons can be generated via adult neurogenesis.
source: These dopaminergic (DA) interneurons can be generated via adult neurogenesis (Adam and Mizrahi, 2011; Bonzano et al., 2016; De Marchis et al., 2007), and the survival of postnatally generated DA cells is activity-dependent (Bonzano et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Adam and Mizrahi, 2011; Bonzano et al., 2016; De Marchis et al., 2007.

claim: The survival of postnatally generated DA cells is activity-dependent.
source: These dopaminergic (DA) interneurons can be generated via adult neurogenesis (Adam and Mizrahi, 2011; Bonzano et al., 2016; De Marchis et al., 2007), and the survival of postnatally generated DA cells is activity-dependent (Bonzano et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bonzano et al., 2014.

claim: Adult-born DA cells contribute to specific olfactory behaviours.
source: Moreover, adult-born DA cells have been shown to contribute to specific olfactory behaviours (Lazarini et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lazarini et al., 2014.

claim: Morphological variability has been demonstrated among OB DA neurons and has been linked to their time of birth.
source: Indeed, morphological variability has been demonstrated among OB DA neurons and has been linked to their time of birth (Halász et al., 1981; Kiyokage et al., 2010; Kosaka and Kosaka, 2007; Kosaka et al., 2008; Kosaka and Kosaka, 2009; Kosaka and Kosaka, 2011; Kosaka and Kosaka, 2016; McLean and Shipley, 1988; Pignatelli and Belluzzi, 2017; Pignatelli et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: No discrete features demarcating distinct OB DA subpopulations have yet been identified.
source: However, no discrete features demarcating distinct OB DA subpopulations have yet been identified.
evidence: This statement is presented as a gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Nothing is currently known regarding the functional properties of putative OB DA subtypes.
source: More importantly, nothing is currently known regarding the functional properties of putative OB DA subtypes.
evidence: This statement is presented as a gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: A subset of large DA neurons possess a clear AnkG-positive AIS.
source: While for most TH-positive cells we could not detect AnkG label on any of their processes, we identified a subset of large DA neurons that possessed a clear AnkG-positive AIS (Figure 1A, middle and right panel; Kosaka et al., 2008).
evidence: This is directly observed in immunohistochemical experiments and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The AISs of OB DA neurons are often thin, short and located rather distally away from the soma.
source: Like their midbrain DA (González-Cabrera et al., 2017; Meza et al., 2018) and cultured (Chand et al., 2015) counterparts, the AISs of OB DA neurons were often thin, short and located rather distally away from the soma.
evidence: This observation is based on immunohistochemical data and is compared to findings in other DA neuron populations cited in the text.

claim: AIS-positive DA cells comprise at least 2.5% of the overall OB DA population.
source: Nevertheless, a lower-bound estimate (see Materials and methods) suggests they comprise at least 2.5% of the overall OB DA population.
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate based on counting AIS-positive cells in immunostained tissue.

claim: The soma area distribution of the general bulbar TH+ population is not unimodal.
source: As shown in Figure 1B, the soma area distribution of the general bulbar TH+ population is clearly not unimodal (blue distribution): most DA cells are relatively small (peak 55 μm2), but there is a distinct minority that are significantly larger (peak 140 μm2) (Kosaka and Kosaka, 2007; McLean and Shipley, 1988; Pignatelli et al., 2005).
evidence: This is shown in the soma area distribution plot in Figure 1B and is consistent with previous studies cited.

claim: Most DA cells are relatively small with a peak soma area of 55 μm2.
source: As shown in Figure 1B, the soma area distribution of the general bulbar TH+ population is clearly not unimodal (blue distribution): most DA cells are relatively small (peak 55 μm2), but there is a distinct minority that are significantly larger (peak 140 μm2) (Kosaka and Kosaka, 2007; McLean and Shipley, 1988; Pignatelli et al., 2005).
evidence: This is shown in the soma area distribution plot in Figure 1B.

claim: A distinct minority of DA cells are significantly larger with a peak soma area of 140 μm2.
source: As shown in Figure 1B, the soma area distribution of the general bulbar TH+ population is clearly not unimodal (blue distribution): most DA cells are relatively small (peak 55 μm2), but there is a distinct minority that are significantly larger (peak 140 μm2) (Kosaka and Kosaka, 2007; McLean and Shipley, 1988; Pignatelli et al., 2005).
evidence: This is shown in the soma area distribution plot in Figure 1B and is consistent with previous studies cited.

claim: Performing soma area analysis solely for TH+/AnkG+ cells produced a unimodal distribution centred on the large-cell peak of the full population curve.
source: In contrast, performing a similar analysis solely for TH+/AnkG+ cells (i.e. DA neurons with an AIS) produced a unimodal distribution centred on the large-cell peak of the full population curve (Figure 1B, magenta line; peak 137 μm2).
evidence: This is shown in the soma area distribution plot in Figure 1B.

claim: Large AIS-positive cells represent a distinct sub-population of OB DA neurons.
source: Large AIS-positive cells therefore represent a distinct sub-population of OB DA neurons.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the soma area distribution data showing a unimodal distribution for AIS-positive cells centered on the large-cell peak.

claim: Large, AIS-positive DA neurons are mostly found in the lower portions of the GL towards the external plexiform layer (EPL) border.
source: AIS-positive DA neurons, however, were mostly found in the lower portions of the GL towards the external plexiform layer (EPL) border, with very little presence in the upper or mid-GL (Figure 1C; Liberia et al., 2012)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and supported by statistical analysis showing significant differences in distribution across GL sub-laminae.

claim: There is a significant effect of sub-lamina × cell type on DA neuron distribution in the GL.
source: effect of sub-lamina ×cell type in two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F3,66 = 35.47, p<0.0001; post-hoc Sidak's test between cell types, upper-GL, p=0.014; mid-GL, p<0.0001; lower-GL, p<0.0001; EPL border, p=0.98; n = 24 slices from N = 3 mice
evidence: This is a statistical result from two-way repeated-measures ANOVA analysis of cell distribution data.

claim: The AIS is crucial for the maintenance of axo-dendritic neuronal polarity.
source: The AIS is crucial for the maintenance of axo-dendritic neuronal polarity (Hedstrom et al., 2008), and is often employed as an indicator of axonal identity (e.g. Watanabe et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hedstrom et al., 2008 and Watanabe et al., 2012.

claim: The AnkG-positive processes of large AIS-containing DA cells co-localise with the axonal marker TRIM-46.
source: First – as a positive control – we confirmed that while the AnkG-positive processes of large AIS-containing DA cells co-localised with the axonal marker TRIM-46 (Figure 2A;van Beuningen et al., 2015)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A with immunohistochemical co-labeling.

claim: The axonal marker TRIM-46 is entirely absent from the processes of small OB DA neurons.
source: this axonal marker was entirely absent from the processes of small OB DA neurons (Figure 2B; n = 10, N = 3, average soma area 58 μm2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B with immunohistochemical labeling in 10 cells from 3 mice.

claim: DA cells with an AIS express MAP-2 in all processes, even in the proximal axon.
source: DA cells with an AIS express MAP-2 in all processes, even in the proximal axon (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C with immunohistochemical labeling.

claim: Proximal axonal MAP-2 expression fades where AnkG expression begins in AIS-positive DA cells.
source: However, as reported for other cell types (Gumy et al., 2017; van Beuningen et al., 2015), this proximal axonal MAP-2 expression fades where AnkG expression begins, and MAP2 is absent from the post-AnkG portion of the axon (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and is consistent with findings in other cell types cited.

claim: AIS-negative DA neurons express MAP-2 along the entire length of all their processes.
source: Conversely, AIS-negative DA neurons express MAP-2 along the entire length of all their processes (Figure 2D; n = 10, N = 3, average soma area 49 μm2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D with immunohistochemical labeling in 10 cells from 3 mice.

claim: The presence of an AIS is indicative of axonal identity in OB DA cells.
source: These data strongly suggest that the presence of an AIS is indicative of axonal identity in OB DA cells, and that the small TH-positive neurons that lack an AIS are truly anaxonic.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined TRIM-46 and MAP-2 labeling data.

claim: Small TH-positive neurons that lack an AIS are truly anaxonic.
source: These data strongly suggest that the presence of an AIS is indicative of axonal identity in OB DA cells, and that the small TH-positive neurons that lack an AIS are truly anaxonic.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined TRIM-46 and MAP-2 labeling data showing absence of axonal markers and presence of dendritic markers in all processes.

claim: Small, anaxonic DA neurons have limited dendritic arborisations that ramify across a small region of the glomerular layer.
source: Small, anaxonic DA neurons had limited dendritic arborisations that ramified across a small region of the glomerular layer (Figure 3B,C,E,F).
evidence: This is shown in morphological reconstructions and Sholl analysis in Figure 3.

claim: The dendrites of large, axon-bearing DA cells are much more broadly spread than those of small, anaxonic DA neurons.
source: By contrast, the dendrites of large, axon-bearing DA cells were much more broadly spread (Figure 3D,E,F).
evidence: This is shown in morphological reconstructions and Sholl analysis in Figure 3.

claim: Quantitative Sholl analysis revealed highly significant cell-type differences on multiple dendritic parameters.
source: Despite considerable cell-to-cell morphological variability within each sub-class (Figure 3E,F), quantitative Sholl analysis (see Materials and methods) revealed highly significant cell-type differences on multiple dendritic parameters (Table 1; Figure 3E; effect of cell type in mixed model ANOVA analysis of Sholl distributions, F1,36 = 5.30, p=0.027).
evidence: This is a statistical result from mixed model ANOVA analysis of Sholl distribution data, with detailed measurements in Table 1.

claim: Glomerular layer interneurons in the OB, including TH-positive DA neurons, belong to the highly restricted group of neuronal types capable of regenerating throughout life via adult neurogenesis.
source: Glomerular layer interneurons in the OB, including TH-positive DA neurons, belong to the highly restricted group of neuronal types capable of regenerating throughout life via adult neurogenesis (Betarbet et al., 1996; Bonzano et al., 2016; De Marchis et al., 2007; Winner et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Data from birthdating experiments suggest that OB DA neurons are not homogeneous in their time of generation based on soma size.
source: However, data from birthdating experiments suggest that – at least on the basis of soma size – OB DA neurons are not homogeneous in their time of generation (Kosaka and Kosaka, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kosaka and Kosaka, 2009.

claim: With increasing birth age, the soma area distributions of DA neurons lose their right-end tail, indicating that large DA neurons are mostly born during early development.
source: The results, presented in Figure 4B–H, clearly show that with increasing birth age the soma area distributions lose their right-end tail, indicating that the large DA neurons are mostly born during early development (Kosaka and Kosaka, 2009).
evidence: This is shown in the soma area distributions for different BrdU injection timepoints in Figure 4B-H and is consistent with previous findings cited.

claim: Soma area in adult-born OB DA neurons appeared small compared to overall DA population distributions at earlier ages.
source: Interestingly, soma area in adult-born OB DA neurons (Figure 4H) appeared small compared to overall DA population distributions at earlier ages, an effect that was not accounted for by either histological processing differences or cell maturation state, and which might indicate a potential specialization of this DA subpopulation that warrants investigation in future studies.
evidence: This observation is based on comparison of soma area distributions in Figure 4H with earlier timepoints.

claim: AIS-positive DA neurons were exclusively born in embryonic development, with a clear peak in their generation at E11-12.
source: AIS-positive DA neurons were exclusively born in embryonic development, with a clear peak in their generation at E11-12 (Figure 4B,C,H) and only very few being produced between E13 and E18 (Figure 4D–F,H).
evidence: This is shown in the BrdU birthdating data in Figure 4B-H, where AIS-positive cells (marked with circles) are only found in embryonic injection timepoints.

claim: No neonatal- or adult-born OB DA neurons possessed an AIS.
source: We did not find a single neonatal- or adult-born OB DA neuron that possessed an AIS (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: This is shown in the BrdU birthdating data in Figure 4G-H, where no AIS-positive cells were found in postnatal or adult injection timepoints.

claim: Very few double-labelled BrdU+/TH+ cells were found 4 months after adult BrdU injection, and all were AIS-negative.
source: We found very few double-labelled BrdU+/TH +cells (Figure 5B; n = 15 cells from N = 2 mice), and all were AIS-negative.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B with BrdU birthdating after a 4-month chase period.

claim: The absence of an AIS in adult-generated DA cells is unlikely due to insufficient maturation time.
source: The absence of an AIS in adult-generated cells is therefore unlikely due to insufficient maturation time, and instead likely reflects a fundamental characteristic of this OB DA subtype.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the finding that even after 4 months, adult-born DA cells still lack an AIS.

claim: There is a preponderance of large AIS-positive DA cells in the neonate.
source: To address the first question, we collected tissue from newborn pups (P0) and quantified the soma area of TH-labelled DA neurons (Figure 6A). We indeed found a right-shifted distribution of larger DA neurons at this early postnatal timepoint (Figure 6B, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test D = 0.3581, p<0.01; McLean and Shipley, 1988).
evidence: This is shown in the soma area distribution comparison between P0 and P28 in Figure 6B, with statistical significance.

claim: The prevalence of AIS-positive DA cells at P0 is approximately 6% of the overall TH-positive population.
source: We also obtained a slightly higher lower-bound estimate for the prevalence of AIS-positive DA cells at P0 (Figure 6C; see Materials and methods), at ~6% of the overall TH-positive population.
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate based on counting AIS-positive cells in P0 tissue.

claim: AIS-positive neurons at P0 already have large soma areas (mean ± SEM 98 ± 5 μm2).
source: In addition, AIS-positive neurons at P0 already have large soma areas (mean ± SEM 98 ± 5 μm2, n = 16, N = 2; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from P0 tissue shown in Figure 6D.

claim: DA neurons born at E12 were still found in the bulb of 6-month-old adult mice.
source: As shown in Figure 7B, we were still able to find DA neurons born at E12 in the bulb of these fully adult mice.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B with BrdU birthdating after a 6-month chase period.

claim: All E12-born DA neurons found in 6-month-old mice were large and the overwhelming majority carried an AIS.
source: All these neurons were large and the overwhelming majority carried an AIS.
evidence: This is shown in the data from 6-month-old mice in Figure 7.

claim: E12-born DA neurons in adult animals (6 months) were larger than those in 1-month-old animals (91 ± 4 μm2).
source: When we compared these adult animals to littermates that had also been injected at E12 but perfused at P28, we found that E12-born DA neurons in adult animals were larger (91 ± 4 μm2; Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is shown in the soma area distribution comparison in Figure 7C,D.

claim: In 1-month-old animals, TH+/E12-BrdU+ cells were relatively abundant but only 25% of them were AIS-positive.
source: Moreover, while in 1-month-old animals TH+/E12-BrdU+ cells were relatively abundant but only 25% of them were AIS-positive, in adult mice TH+/E12-BrdU+ cells were rare but over 90% of them possessed an AIS (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 7E comparing 1-month and 6-month-old mice.

claim: In adult mice (6 months), TH+/E12-BrdU+ cells were rare but over 90% of them possessed an AIS.
source: Moreover, while in 1-month-old animals TH+/E12-BrdU+ cells were relatively abundant but only 25% of them were AIS-positive, in adult mice TH+/E12-BrdU+ cells were rare but over 90% of them possessed an AIS (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 7E comparing 1-month and 6-month-old mice.

claim: Of the mixed pool of DA neurons born at E12, the initially abundant AIS-negative cells are turned over at some point before 6 months of age, to be substituted by postnatally-born AIS-negative neurons.
source: These findings strongly suggest that, of the mixed pool of DA neurons born at E12, the initially abundant AIS-negative cells are turned over at some point before 6 months of age, to be substituted by postnatallyborn AIS-negative neurons.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the change in proportion of AIS-positive vs AIS-negative E12-born cells between 1 month and 6 months.

claim: Embryonically-generated, large AIS-positive cells can persist throughout adult life.
source: In contrast, embryonicallygenerated, large AIS-positive cells can persist throughout adult life.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the finding that E12-born AIS-positive cells are still present at 6 months of age.

claim: In DAT-tdT mice, the majority of TH+ DA cells also expressed tdT (90 ± 4% of all TH+ neurons were also tdT+).
source: In the resulting DAT-tdT mice, the majority of TH+ DA cells also expressed tdT (90 ± 4% of all TH+ neurons were also tdT+; n = 369, N = 3; Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from immunohistochemical analysis in DAT-tdT mice shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The rare TH+ neurons that lacked tdT fluorescence tended to be large.
source: The rare TH+ neurons that lacked tdT fluorescence tended to be large (Figure 8B), suggesting that while our genetic labelling strategy comprehensively identified small, anaxonic DA neurons, it under-represented the large, AIS-positive DA subtype.
evidence: This is shown in the soma size distribution in Figure 8B.

claim: Only 67% of TH+/AIS+ DA neurons also expressed tdT.
source: Indeed, co-label for AnkG revealed that only 67% of TH+/AIS+ DA neurons also expressed tdT (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 8B inset.

claim: There was no difference in soma size between TH+/AIS+/tdT+ and TH+/AIS+/tdT- neurons.
source: However, tdT expression did not appear to reveal any further subdivision amongst the large, AIS-positive DA cells, because we found no difference in soma size between TH+/AIS+/tdT+ and TH+/AIS+/tdT- neurons (tdT+, mean ± SEM 118 ± 10 µm2; tdT-, 126 ± 5 µm2; Welch's corrected t21.12 = 0.66, p=0.52).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of soma sizes between tdT+ and tdT- AIS-positive cells.

claim: Biphasic neurons were significantly larger than their monophasic counterparts.
source: Indeed, we found that biphasic neurons were significantly larger than their monophasic counterparts (Figure 8F; Table 2; [Chand et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is shown in the soma area quantification in Figure 8F and Table 2, and is consistent with previous findings cited.

claim: Biphasic cells generated single APs in response to lower amplitude somatic current injection than monophasic cells.
source: Biphasic neurons generated single APs in response to lower amplitude somatic current injection, and initiated those APs more rapidly (Figure 8F; Table 2).
evidence: This is shown in the current threshold quantification in Figure 8F and Table 2.

claim: Biphasic cells initiated APs more rapidly than monophasic cells.
source: Biphasic neurons generated single APs in response to lower amplitude somatic current injection, and initiated those APs more rapidly (Figure 8F; Table 2).
evidence: This is shown in the onset rapidness quantification in Figure 8F and Table 2.

claim: Biphasic cells displayed a linear input-output curve when induced to fire repeatedly.
source: When induced to fire repeatedly in response to longer lasting 500 ms somatic current injections of increasing intensity, biphasic cells displayed a linear input-output curve.
evidence: This is shown in the input-output curves in Figure 8G.

claim: Monophasic cells could not produce a linear increase in spike number and soon reached a firing plateau.
source: Conversely, monophasic cells could not produce such a linear increase in spike number and soon reached a firing plateau (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is shown in the input-output curves in Figure 8G.

claim: Monophasic cells had a significantly lower slope of their input-output curve than biphasic cells.
source: This resulted in monophasic cells having a significantly lower slope of their input-output curve, and a significantly lower maximum number of fired APs (Figure 8H; Table 2).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 8H and Table 2.

claim: Monophasic cells had a significantly lower maximum number of fired APs than biphasic cells.
source: This resulted in monophasic cells having a significantly lower slope of their input-output curve, and a significantly lower maximum number of fired APs (Figure 8H; Table 2).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 8H and Table 2.

claim: Using k-means classification, recorded cells could be assigned to either the mono- or biphasic group with 85% accuracy.
source: Furthermore, using a k-means classification approach with the same data (see Materials and methods) we were able to assign our recorded cells to either the mono- or biphasic group with 85% accuracy.
evidence: This is shown in the PCA and k-means classification analysis in Figure 8I.

claim: When taken together, functional properties reveal a significant distinction between putative AIS-positive and putative AIS-negative cell types.
source: This suggests that, although there is considerable overlap in the functional properties of different subclasses of OB DA neuron, when taken together those properties reveal a significant distinction between putative AIS-positive and putative AIS-negative cell types.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the PCA and k-means classification analysis showing clear clustering by cell type.

claim: Early excitatory responses were the most prevalent form of odour-evoked signal in DAT-GCaMP neurons (at least one early excitatory response was observed in 631/1216 = 52% of cells).
source: In many cases, a given odorant stimulus produced a relatively rapid increase in GCaMP fluorescence that then decayed back towards baseline – these responses, which we termed 'early excitatory' events, were the most prevalent form of odour-evoked signal in our DAT-GCaMP neurons (at least one early excitatory response was observed in 631/1216 = 52% of cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from in vivo GCaMP imaging experiments.

claim: Late excitatory events were less frequent than early excitatory events (245/1216 = 20% of cells had at least one late excitatory response).
source: In other cases, stimuli produced an increase in GCaMP intensity that had a delayed onset and peaked late in a given recording sweep – these 'late excitatory' events were readily and objectively distinguishable from early excitatory events (see Materials and methods; Figure 9C,D) and were less frequent in our sample (245/1216 = 20% of cells had at least one late excitatory response).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from in vivo GCaMP imaging experiments.

claim: Inhibitory events were observed in 296/1216 = 24% of cells.
source: Finally, we observed reasonably common examples of decreased GCaMP fluorescence upon odorant presentation. These 'inhibitory' events (at least one seen in 296/1216 = 24% of cells) usually had delayed onset
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from in vivo GCaMP imaging experiments.

claim: Peak latencies for all response types had coefficients of variation that were significantly less than one, indicative of non-random event timing across individual stimulus repeats.
source: Peak latencies for all response types had coefficients of variation that were significantly less than one, indicative of non-random event timing across individual stimulus repeats (Figure 9F; early excitatory, mean ±SEM 0.28 ± 0.0063, Wilcoxon test vs 1, W = −198733, p<0.0001; late excitatory 0.40 ± 0.017, W = −29773, p<0.0001; inhibitory 0.38 ± 0.015, W = −42085, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of response reliability from in vivo GCaMP imaging data shown in Figure 9F.

claim: Mean amplitudes for the two stimulus repeats that produced the weakest responses were still significantly greater than one standard deviation above baseline for all response types.
source: In addition, no response type was generated by spurious, one-off fluctuations in fluorescence – mean amplitudes for the two stimulus repeats that produced the weakest responses were still significantly greater than one standard deviation above baseline (Figure 9G; early excitatory, mean ±SEM 5.38 ± 0.26, Wilcoxon test vs 1, W = 198036, p<0.0001; late excitatory 2.29 ± 0.20, W = 17963, p<0.0001; inhibitory 1.28 ± 0.060, W = 12954, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of response reliability from in vivo GCaMP imaging data shown in Figure 9G.

claim: Response reliability measures did not differ between small and big DA neurons for late excitatory and inhibitory events.
source: Crucially, neither of these measures of response reliability differed between small and big DA neurons, showing that late excitatory and inhibitory events were not only reliable per se, but were also just as reliable in both cell types (peak time CV, late excitatory, fixed effect of cell-type in multilevel ANOVA, F1,232 = 1.89, p=0.17; inhibitory, F1,289 = 0.12, p=0.75; mean amplitude of 2 weakest responses, late excitatory, F1,212 = 0.83, p=0.36; inhibitory, F1,177 = 0.19, p=0.67).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis from multilevel ANOVA comparing response reliability between cell types.

claim: 67% of imaged DAT-GCaMP+ cells displayed at least one response type evoked by at least one of the eight odour stimuli.
source: Overall, 817/1216 = 67% of imaged DAT-GCaMP+ cells displayed at least one response type evoked by at least one of the eight odour stimuli we used.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from in vivo GCaMP imaging experiments.

claim: There was no significant difference in the proportions of small vs big DA neurons that displayed at least one odorant-evoked fast excitatory response.
source: Paired, within-animal comparisons for the three major response types across the 13 mice in our sample revealed no significant differences in the proportions of small vs big DA neurons that displayed at least one odorant-evoked fast excitatory (Figure 9H; small cells, mean ±SEM 46 ± 7%; big cells 51 ± 6%; paired t-test, t12 = 1.10, p=0.29)
evidence: This is a statistical comparison from paired t-test analysis shown in Figure 9H.

claim: There was no significant difference in the proportions of small vs big DA neurons that displayed at least one odorant-evoked slow excitatory response.
source: or slow excitatory (Figure 9H; small cells, 19 ± 3%; big cells 23 ± 3%; paired t-test, t12 = 1.15, p=0.27) response.
evidence: This is a statistical comparison from paired t-test analysis shown in Figure 9H.

claim: A significantly higher proportion of inhibitory-responding neurons was found amongst the big cell population compared to small cells.
source: However, we did see a significantly higher proportion of inhibitory-responding neurons amongst the big cell population (Figure 9H; small cells, 16 ± 4%; big cells 26 ± 6%; Wilcoxon test, W13 = 62, p=0.012).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison from Wilcoxon test analysis shown in Figure 9H.

claim: The mean TI value for all excitatory responses (early + late combined) was 1.99 across all neurons.
source: The mean TI value for all excitatory responses (early + late combined) was 1.99 across all neurons in our sample, rising to 3.29 within the subset of neurons that displayed at least one excitatory response.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of tuning index from in vivo GCaMP imaging data.

claim: There were only very weak correlations between TI measures calculated for the three major forms of odour-evoked response.
source: Importantly, we found only very weak correlations between TI measures calculated for the three major forms of odour-evoked response (early excitatory vs late excitatory, Spearman r = 0.018, p=0.53; early excitatory vs inhibitory, r = 0.13, p<0.0001; late excitatory vs inhibitory, r = 0.030, p=0.30; n = 1216 in all cases)
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of correlations between different tuning index measures.

claim: There was no effect of cell type on early excitatory TI values.
source: Using this approach, we found no effect of cell type on early excitatory TI values (Figure 10B; fixed effect of cell-type in multilevel ANOVA, F1,1180 = 2.04, p=0.15).
evidence: This is a statistical result from multilevel ANOVA analysis shown in Figure 10B.

claim: For both late excitatory and inhibitory response types, the effect of cell type on TI was significant, with big cells possessing consistently larger TI values.
source: For both late excitatory and inhibitory response types, though, the effect of cell type on TI was significant (Figure 10B; late excitatory, F1,1214 = 5.58, p=0.018; inhibitory, F1,1143 = 6.92, p=0.009), with big cells possessing consistently larger TI values on a mouse-by-mouse basis.
evidence: This is a statistical result from multilevel ANOVA analysis shown in Figure 10B.

claim: When responding to odorant stimuli with late excitatory or inhibitory events, big OB DA cells are significantly more broadly tuned than their small-soma neighbours.
source: When responding to odorant stimuli with late excitatory or inhibitory events, therefore, big OB DA cells are significantly more broadly tuned than their small-soma neighbours.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the multilevel ANOVA analysis showing higher TI values for late excitatory and inhibitory responses in big cells.

claim: Big cells had significantly weaker responses to odorant stimuli than small cells, an effect that held across all response types.
source: Actually, measures of event amplitudes revealed the opposite to be the case: big cells had significantly weaker responses to odorant stimuli, a highly significant effect that held across all response types (Figure 10C; early excitatory, fixed effect of cell-type in multilevel ANOVA, F1,626 = 6.58, p=0.011; late excitatory, F1,244 = 4.50, p=0.035; inhibitory, F1,295 = 32.69, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from multilevel ANOVA analysis shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Resting fluorescence was significantly higher in big cells than in small cells.
source: Additionally, it could be related to another feature of in vivo GCaMP activity: baseline fluorescence. Resting fluorescence was significantly higher in big cells (fixed effect of cell-type in multilevel ANOVA, F1,658 = 12.00, p=0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical result from multilevel ANOVA analysis of baseline fluorescence.

claim: Baseline noise was significantly lower in big cells than in small cells.
source: while baseline noise was significantly lower in this cell type (F1,1211 = 41.84, p<0.0001)
evidence: This is a statistical result from multilevel ANOVA analysis of baseline noise.

claim: Both baseline fluorescence and baseline noise correlated strongly with all response amplitude measures.
source: and both measures, especially noise, correlated strongly with all response amplitude measures (baseline fluorescence vs early excitatory amplitude, Spearman r = −0.49, p<0.0001, n = 612; vs late excitatory amplitude, r = −0.44, p<0.0001, n = 235; vs inhibitory amplitude, r = −0.58, p<0.0001, n = 282; baseline noise vs early excitatory amplitude, r = 0.67, p<0.0001, n = 631; vs late excitatory amplitude, r = 0.72, p<0.0001, n = 245; vs inhibitory amplitude, r = 0.83, p<0.0001, n = 296).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of correlations between baseline measures and response amplitudes.

claim: Cell-type distinctions in baseline activity cannot account for the differences in response selectivity between big and small cell populations.
source: However, these cell-type distinctions in baseline activity cannot account for the differences in response selectivity between big and small cell populations (Figure 10B).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that early excitatory tuning was identical between cell types despite baseline differences, and from weak correlations between baseline measures and TI values.

claim: There was no difference in decay kinetics between big and small OB DA cells for late excitatory responses.
source: We found slow decay constants of approximately 8–11 s for both late excitatory and inhibitory response types, but no difference in decay kinetics between big and small OB DA cells (Figure 10—figure supplement 1C,D; late excitatory, fixed effect of cell type in multilevel ANOVA, F1,98 = 0.32, p=0.57; inhibitory, F1,113 = 0.078, p=0.78).
evidence: This is a statistical result from multilevel ANOVA analysis shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Big/putative AIS-positive and small/putative AIS-negative OB DA neurons differ significantly in the broader selectivity of big cells for specific odour-evoked response types.
source: Overall in terms of odorant response properties, therefore, big/putative AIS-positive and small/putative AIS-negative OB DA neurons differ significantly in: 1) the broader selectivity of big cells for specific odour-evoked response types
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the in vivo GCaMP imaging data.

claim: Big/putative AIS-positive and small/putative AIS-negative OB DA neurons differ significantly in the higher resting fluorescence, lower baseline noise, and smaller response amplitudes of big cells.
source: and 2) the higher resting fluorescence, lower baseline noise, and smaller response amplitudes of big cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the in vivo GCaMP imaging data.

claim: The two major functional features (broader selectivity and baseline/amplitude differences) appear to be largely independent of each other.
source: Moreover, these two major functional features appear to be largely independent of each other.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that early excitatory tuning was identical between cell types despite baseline differences, and from weak correlations between baseline measures and TI values.

claim: The majority of DA cells are small, locally projecting, anaxonic neurons which fire low numbers of somatic action potentials.
source: The majority of DA cells are small, locally projecting, anaxonic neurons which fire low numbers of somatic action potentials; they are continuously generated and turned over throughout life, and have stronger odorant-evoked responses that for certain event types are more narrowly tuned.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating multiple findings from the study.

claim: Small, anaxonic DA cells are continuously generated and turned over throughout life.
source: The majority of DA cells are small, locally projecting, anaxonic neurons which fire low numbers of somatic action potentials; they are continuously generated and turned over throughout life, and have stronger odorant-evoked responses that for certain event types are more narrowly tuned.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating findings from birthdating experiments and in vivo imaging.

claim: Small, anaxonic DA cells have stronger odorant-evoked responses that for certain event types are more narrowly tuned.
source: The majority of DA cells are small, locally projecting, anaxonic neurons which fire low numbers of somatic action potentials; they are continuously generated and turned over throughout life, and have stronger odorant-evoked responses that for certain event types are more narrowly tuned.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating findings from in vivo GCaMP imaging.

claim: A minority of DA cells are large, wide-branching and equipped with an axon and an AIS, from which they generate high-frequency discharges of action potentials.
source: Conversely, a minority of DA cells are large, wide-branching and equipped with an axon and an AIS, from which they generate high-frequency discharges of action potentials.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating multiple findings from the study.

claim: AIS-positive DA cells are born exclusively during early embryonic development and persist throughout life.
source: These AIS-positive DA cells are born exclusively during early embryonic development and persist throughout life
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating findings from birthdating experiments.

claim: The high excitability of AIS-positive DA cells is associated with weaker sensory-evoked responses in vivo, some types of which are more broadly tuned to odorant stimuli.
source: their high excitability is nevertheless associated with weaker sensory-evoked responses in vivo, some types of which are more broadly tuned to odorant stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating findings from electrophysiology and in vivo imaging.

claim: Cell-type identity is intimately linked to the functional role that any neuron can play in a given circuit.
source: Cell-type identity – as determined by ontology, gene expression, morphology, connectivity, and/or physiology – is intimately linked to the functional role that any neuron can play in a given circuit.
evidence: This is a general statement about neuroscience principles presented in the discussion.

claim: Broad cell-type distinctions must be supplemented by fine-scale subdivisions within different cell types in order to fully understand network function.
source: These studies show that broad cell-type distinctions must be supplemented by fine-scale subdivisions within different cell types in order to fully understand network function.
evidence: This statement is presented as a conclusion drawn from recent comprehensive cell-type classification studies.

claim: In glomerular layer circuits, glutamatergic, vGlut-expressing external tufted cells are readily distinguished from their GABA-positive interneuron neighbours.
source: In glomerular layer circuits – the first networks to process sensory information arriving from the periphery – there is at least broad consensus on the division of juxtaglomerular neurons into excitatory and inhibitory cell types: glutamatergic, vGlut-expressing external tufted cells are, on the whole, readily distinguished from their GABA-positive interneuron neighbours (Hayar et al., 2004, but see Tatti et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hayar et al., 2004 and Tatti et al., 2014.

claim: Amongst GABAergic interneurons in the glomerular layer are three neurochemically-distinct subpopulations, distinguishable by their non-overlapping expression of calretinin, calbindin, and tyrosine hydroxylase.
source: Furthermore, amongst those GABAergic interneurons are three neurochemically-distinct subpopulations, distinguishable (at least in mouse) by their non-overlapping expression of calretinin, calbindin, and tyrosine hydroxylase (Kosaka and Kosaka, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kosaka and Kosaka, 2007.

claim: It has long been recognised that TH-positive OB DA neurons are highly heterogeneous.
source: However, although it has long been recognised that this latter group of TH-positive OB DA neurons are highly heterogeneous (Davis and Macrides, 1983; Halász et al., 1981; Kosaka and Kosaka, 2007; Pignatelli et al., 2005), there has been significant disagreement as to the precise nature of cell sub-type identity within this population.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: There is as yet no definitive classification of OB DA neurons.
source: There is as yet no definitive classification of OB DA neurons, even though such a scheme is vital for our understanding of sensory processing functions in glomerular circuits.
evidence: This statement is presented as a gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: The AIS-negative class of OB DA neurons shares important morphological features with a population of DAT-expressing 'clasping SACs' identified by recent live imaging.
source: The AIS-negative class also shares important morphological features with a population of DAT-expressing 'clasping SACs' identified by recent live imaging of intracellular fills in acute OB slices (Bywalez et al., 2016), whose distinct dendritic architecture and predominantly juxtaglomerular arborisations would appear to separate them from classically-defined PGCs (Kosaka and Kosaka, 2016; Pinching and Powell, 1971).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bywalez et al., 2016, Kosaka and Kosaka, 2016, and Pinching and Powell, 1971.

claim: Segregating OB DA neurons based on axonal criteria has enabled important functional distinctions to be identified between subgroups that were not evident from previous divisions based on continuous measures.
source: Indeed, segregating OB DA neurons based on axonal criteria has enabled important functional distinctions to be identified between subgroups (Figure 8; [Chand et al., 2015]) that were not evident from previous divisions based on continuous measures (Pignatelli and Belluzzi, 2017; Pignatelli et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by the current study's findings and citations to previous studies.

claim: Both AIS-positive and AIS-negative DA subtypes possess dendritic processes that ramify within the glomerular neuropil.
source: Both AIS-positive and AIS-negative DA subtypes possess dendritic processes that ramify within the glomerular neuropil (Figure 3)
evidence: This is shown in the morphological reconstructions in Figure 3.

claim: Both AIS-positive and AIS-negative DA subtypes have the potential to contribute to intraglomerular inhibition, assuming that the release of GABA and/or dopamine occurs from their dendrites.
source: so, assuming that the release of GABA and/or dopamine occurs from these dendrites in both cell types (Borisovska et al., 2013; Kiyokage et al., 2017; Vaaga et al., 2017, but see Liberia et al., 2012), both subpopulations have the potential to contribute to intraglomerular inhibition.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on morphological observations and cited literature about dendritic release.

claim: GABA and/or dopamine can inhibit release probability at OSN presynaptic terminals via the activation of GABAB and D2 receptors, respectively.
source: This includes GABA and/or dopamine inhibiting release probability at OSN presynaptic terminals via the activation of GABAB and D2 receptors, respectively (Ennis et al., 2001; Hsia et al., 1999; Korshunov et al., 2017; McGann, 2013; Vaaga et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Local GABA release can provide a brake on recurrent excitatory glomerular networks.
source: Local GABA release can also provide a brake on recurrent excitatory glomerular networks (Gire and Schoppa, 2009; Murphy et al., 2005; Najac et al., 2011)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gire and Schoppa, 2009; Murphy et al., 2005; Najac et al., 2011.

claim: Local GABA release can effect auto-disinhibition at high input strengths.
source: as well as effecting auto-disinhibition at high input strengths (Parsa et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Parsa et al., 2015.

claim: Intraglomerular inhibition produced by both subtypes of OB DA neuron may subserve highly local gain control, potentially acting as a high-pass temporal and contrast filter to facilitate the detection of strong odorant stimuli.
source: By acting at the levels of both input terminals and projection neuron dendrites, intraglomerular inhibition produced by both subtypes of OB DA neuron may subserve highly local gain control, potentially acting as a high-pass temporal and contrast filter to facilitate the detection of strong odorant stimuli (e.g. Banerjee et al., 2015; Cavarretta et al., 2016; Cleland and Sethupathy, 2006; Gire and Schoppa, 2009; Korshunov et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about functional roles supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Interglomerular inhibition would appear to be restricted solely to the subpopulation of large, deep-lying, highly excitable AIS-positive OB DA neurons.
source: Interglomerular inhibition, by contrast, would appear to be restricted solely to the subpopulation of large, deep-lying, highly excitable AIS-positive OB DA neurons.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the morphological finding that only AIS-positive cells have axons that can project between glomeruli.

claim: Only the population of large, AIS-positive GABAergic GL interneurons has an axonal process that can signal sufficient distances between glomerular networks.
source: Quite simply, only this population of GABAergic GL interneurons has an axonal process that can signal sufficient distances between glomerular networks (Figures 1, 2 and 3; Kiyokage et al., 2010; Kosaka and Kosaka, 2008).
evidence: This is based on the morphological data showing axons only in AIS-positive cells, supported by citations.

claim: Lateral inhibition between glomeruli has been predicted to enhance contrast between individual stimulus representations, and therefore aid odorant identification and/or discrimination.
source: Given the distribution of odorant information across glomeruli in a spatial map for odour identity (Murthy, 2011), such lateral inhibition between glomeruli has been predicted to enhance contrast between individual stimulus representations, and therefore aid odorant identification and/or discrimination (e.g. Linster and Cleland, 2004; Uchida et al., 2000; Urban, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies and theoretical work.

claim: AIS-positive DA neurons can distribute lateral signals via well-described long-range GABAergic monosynaptic connections onto external tufted cells.
source: This lateral signal could be distributed by AIS-positive DA neurons via well-described long-range GABAergic monosynaptic connections onto external tufted cells (Banerjee et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2013; Whitesell et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Banerjee et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2013; Whitesell et al., 2013.

claim: The distal interglomerular projections of AIS-positive OB DAs can induce rebound excitation via dopaminergic D1-receptor activation.
source: In addition, the distal interglomerular projections of (AIS-positive) OB DAs can induce rebound excitation via dopaminergic D1-receptor activation (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2013.

claim: The delayed DA-mediated effect from AIS-positive cells could contribute to the complex modulation of interglomerular dynamics, especially in the later stages of stimulus processing.
source: Together with these cells' slightly more broadly-tuned late excitatory and delayed inhibitory responses to odorant stimuli (Figure 10), this delayed DA-mediated effect could contribute to the complex modulation of interglomerular dynamics, especially in the later stages of stimulus processing.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about functional roles based on the study's findings and previous literature.

claim: Early in postnatal development, when neuronal activity contributes to the refinement of both OSN terminals and projection neuron dendrites to individual glomeruli, the large, interglomerular-projecting AIS-positive DA cell type is relatively more numerous.
source: Early in postnatal development, when neuronal activity contributes to the refinement of both OSN terminals (Yu et al., 2004; Zou et al., 2004) and projection neuron dendrites (Lin et al., 2000; Matsutani and Yamamoto, 2000) to individual glomeruli, the large, interglomerular-projecting AIS-positive DA cell type is relatively more numerous (Figure 6B).
evidence: This statement is supported by the P0 data in Figure 6B and citations to previous studies about developmental refinement.

claim: Large, AIS-positive DA cells may play a crucial role in co-ordinating odour-evoked and/or spontaneous activity across the glomerular layer at early postnatal ages, allowing distinct activity patterns to drive anatomical segregation at the individual glomerulus level.
source: Maybe these inhibitory interneurons play a crucial role in co-ordinating odour-evoked and/or spontaneous activity across the glomerular layer at these early ages, allowing distinct activity patterns to drive anatomical segregation at the individual glomerulus level.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential developmental roles based on the finding of higher prevalence of AIS-positive cells at P0.

claim: With the notable exception of hippocampal dentate granule cells, it appears that all CNS neurons constitutively born during adulthood are anaxonic.
source: In fact, with the notable exception of hippocampal dentate granule cells, it appears that all CNS neurons constitutively born during adulthood are anaxonic, contributing purely to local network activity by releasing neurotransmitter from their dendrites.
evidence: This is a generalization based on the current findings and knowledge of adult neurogenesis in different brain regions.

claim: It may be simpler for a newly generated neuron to insert itself in a pre-existing network without having to extend and connect a far-reaching axonal process.
source: Indeed, one may speculate that it is simpler for a newly generated neuron to insert itself in a pre-existing network without having to extend and connect a far-reaching axonal process.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential advantages of anaxonic morphology for adult-born neurons.

claim: The large, axonic OB DA cells that need to form extensive connections are born only during early development at the same time that other projection neurons are populating the bulb.
source: Accordingly, the large, axonic OB DA cells that do need to form such extensive connections are born only during early development at the same time that other projection neurons are populating the bulb (Treloar et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by the birthdating data and a citation to Treloar et al., 2010.

claim: Immature adult-born neurons are distinguished by their heightened potential for activity-dependent plasticity.
source: Immature adult-born neurons are distinguished by their heightened potential for activity-dependent plasticity (Livneh and Mizrahi, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Livneh and Mizrahi, 2012.

claim: A local intraglomerular gain control mechanism that can be readily modified by experience allows for broader behavioural flexibility, and permits rapid adaptation to new conditions in the external world.
source: We might hypothesise, then, that a local intraglomerular gain control mechanism that can be readily modified by experience allows for broader behavioural flexibility, and permits rapid adaptation to new conditions in the external world (Lazarini et al., 2014; Livneh and Mizrahi, 2012; Rochefort et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about functional advantages supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: If adult neurogenesis can be seen as an extreme form of structural plasticity that only one subtype of DA cells is capable of performing, it is probably reasonable to assume that more standard and less dramatic forms of plasticity are also differentially expressed by anaxonic and axonic cells.
source: Moreover, if adult neurogenesis can be seen as an extreme form of structural plasticity that only one subtype of DA cells is capable of performing, it is probably reasonable to assume that more standard and less dramatic forms of plasticity are also differentially expressed by anaxonic and axonic cells.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential differences in plasticity mechanisms between cell types.

claim: Cells that do not have an AIS cannot undergo AIS plasticity.
source: By definition, cells that do not have an AIS cannot undergo AIS plasticity
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the absence of the AIS structure in anaxonic cells.

claim: In vitro evidence suggests that large axonic OB DA cells are capable of regulating the length and position of their AISs in an activity-dependent manner.
source: while in vitro evidence suggests that large axonic OB DA cells are capable of regulating the length and position of their AISs in an activity-dependent manner (Chand et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chand et al., 2015.
